source_locator: R588: p. 169; R185: list of commanders
current_activity: Rommel badly injured; Kluge, the OB West commander, takes over Army Group B as well
notes: Event date: Rommel was injured in a car accident on the afternoon of 17 July when an Allied plane strafed his car; that evening, when the news became known, Kluge assumed command of Army Group B in addition to OB West (Breakout and Pursuit ch. 8 p. 169). Wikipedia's Army Group B page gives Kluge as commander from 17 July. Event support: the event itself is stated in the cited text (see Event date); only the headquarters place is a representative point. Location support fallback: no source read gives the headquarters place for 17 July; the point is the Chateau de La Roche-Guyon, the headquarters of claims C0011 and C0202, used as a representative point. Review (German Batch 1b, 27 October 2026): put into conflict group G021 with the new row C0767: the Schramm OKW war diary chronology (p. 458) has Kluge leading Army Group B "ab 19. 7.", two days after the 17 July of this row; this row stays preferred (two sources, the CMH and Wikipedia, against one) without a source that settles the difference; no value of this row changed. Review (cleanup of open items, 28 October 2026; status and values unchanged): the Lexikon der Wehrmacht page of Army Group B (R185) lists Kluge as commander from "19. Juli 1944", the date of C0767, and ends Rommel's tenure on 17 July (the page prints the year 1943, evidently a misprint for 1944). The 19 July date therefore rests on two families (Schramm and the Lexikon) and the 17 July date on two (the CMH and Wikipedia), so the reason given above for preferring this row, two sources against one, no longer holds. This row stays preferred because the CMH text states the takeover itself on the evening of the accident, while the Lexikon gives a tenure date. The two dates fit two event definitions (leading the army group in fact from 17 July, a listed tenure from 19 July), but no source read says so, and the group stays open.

current_activity: Bluecoat: advances from the Caumont ridge at about 07:00 with the 6th Guards Tank Brigade towards Point 309

current_activity: Bluecoat: armoured cars find the Souleuvre bridge intact; the division crosses and holds a bridgehead at Le Beny-Bocage
notes: Event date: 31 July 1944 (Ellis, vol. I, pp. 393, 394). Event support: one source family (Ellis, the British official history). Ellis, Victory in the West, vol. I, p. 393: "Next morning the 21st Panzer Division made several attempts to assemble"; p. 394: "enabled 11th Armoured Division to push troops across the river that night and reach the hills west of le Bény- Bocage; a good bridgehead was formed and the slopes of Point 205 occupied". Location: Le Bény-Bocage, Calvados (new place) with a precision of 3 km. Location approximate: the point is Le Beny-Bocage, the town beside the bridgehead; the bridge itself is about two miles to the west. Location support: Ellis names the Souleuvre bridge two miles west of Le Beny-Bocage and the hills west of the town (p. 394).

notes: Event date: Breakout-18 p343 (Third Army operational at noon, 1 August, with VIII Corps in the Pontaubault–Avranches area). Event definition: the army becomes operational. Location: local-history sources (KilroyTrip, normandie1944) place Patton's Third Army headquarters in an orchard at Néhou from 6 July to about 2 August 1944, so the headquarters was at Néhou on 1 August; the Green Book does not give the location. Coordinates: OpenStreetMap Nominatim centroid of Néhou (the orchard is not located). Relationship: 12th Army Group assigned (Breakout-18 p343). Previously this row carried an Avranches area point (50 km) because no headquarters location had been found. Batch 2 check: the Néhou memorial text (uswarmemorials.org) says Patton's command post was in the village from 6 July to 2 August 1944, and the CMH command-post list (World War II by Day) puts Third Army at Bricquebec-en-Cotentin, about 8 km away, from 26 July to 1 August with Folligny from 2 August (C0486). The two sources agree on the area and the departure date, so confidence is 0.7; the Néhou centroid is kept. Batch 2 review: event support is high (Breakout-18 p343: Third Army operational under Patton at noon on 1 August). Locality support is moderate: three local sources (KilroyTrip, normandie1944, the Néhou memorial) put the headquarters at Néhou, while the CMH list names Bricquebec, about 8 km away, so the precision radius is widened from 5 to 10 km to cover both. The coordinate is the Néhou village centroid and the orchard is not located. The 0.7 follows the rubric for an approximate location with two source families; it is a composite score and does not mean a 70% chance that the command post stood at these coordinates. Event support: high (Green Book, noon 1 August). Location support: moderate (village centroid, sources differ by 8 km).

current_activity: Hodges assumes command as First Army passes to 12th Army Group
notes: Event date: Breakout-18 p343: at noon on 1 August the 12th Army Group became operational, General Hodges assumed command of First Army and Third Army came to life. Event definition: change of First Army commander (Bradley to Hodges) and of its parent headquarters (21st Army Group to 12th Army Group). Location: the Vouilly plaque and normandie44lamemoire say the army headquarters moved to Vouilly on 2 July and stayed until 2 August (a local memorial inaugurated in 2018-2019). The CMH list (World War II by Day) has Saint-Gilles from 1 August and Isigny (which includes Vouilly) from 5 July. Review (Batch 2 corrections): C0484 and C0485 were a conflict group, G015. The two sources do not exclude each other: one says the headquarters left Vouilly on 2 August, the other dates the Saint-Gilles entry to 1 August, 23 km away. They fit a move on 1-2 August, with the order of events within those two days not documented (an advance echelon, the main headquarters, or the list's arrival date convention), so G015 is dissolved and C0485 is the next headquarters location, not an alternative. This row keeps Vouilly because the plaque places the headquarters there through 1 August. Relationship: 12th Army Group assigned from 1 August; 21st Army Group control ended 31 July (C0483). Event support: high (Green Book, noon 1 August). Location support: moderate (local memorial; CMH list differs by a day and 23 km).

current_activity: Panzer Group West reorganized as Fifth Panzer Army (Wikipedia date)
notes: Event date: Wikipedia's Fifth Panzer Army page: 'On August 1, 1944, the remaining elements of Panzer Group West were reorganized as the 5th Panzer Army, with a combat formation remaining in action under the title Panzer Group Eberbach'. current_activity: 2nd Panzer Division attack toward the Brécey-St. Hilaire road stopped at le Mesnil-Adelée

notes: Event date: 14 August 1944, about 11:42 (Stacey, pp. 240-241). Stacey, The Victory Campaign, p. 240: "the start-line, to be crossed at H Hour, was a line running slightly north of Estrees-la-Campagne and through Soignolles"; p. 241: "On the 3rd Division front on the right most of the tanks of two squadrons of the 1st Hussars suffered the former fate; the reserve squadron discovered a crossing at Rouvres"; "Late in the afternoon the armoured advance on this front was proceeding beyond the Laison". Location: Rouvres, Calvados with a precision of 5 km. Location approximate: the Laison crossings (Rouvres, Maizieres, Ernes) lie along a line a few miles long; the point is one of them. Location support: Stacey names Rouvres as the crossing found on the right of the Laison on the first day (p. 241). Commander: Lt.-Gen. G. G. Simonds (Stacey, Appendix G, p. 664: 30 Jan. 44 to 25 Jun. 45). current_activity: Canadian Scottish take Point 168 north of Falaise in a costly afternoon attack; 7th Brigade on Point 159 next day
notes: Event date: 15 August 1944 (Stacey, p. 249). Event definition: On the second day of the advance towards Falaise the 1st Canadian Scottish Regiment, under the 2nd Armoured Brigade, takes Point 168 east of the Falaise road with its heaviest casualties of the campaign so far; on 16 August the 7th Brigade is on the high ground about Point 159 (p. 250). Event support: one source family (Stacey, the Canadian official history). Stacey, The Victory Campaign, p. 249: "On the ridge immediately east of the Falaise Road the 1st Battalion Canadian Scottish Regiment, fighting under command of the 2nd Armoured Brigade, and supported by the 1st Hussars, met and beat down tenacious opposition on Point 168"; p. 250: "Meanwhile the 3rd Division had pushed south from Point 168 and the 7th Brigade occupied the high ground about Point 159"; p. 248: "On the morning of the 15th our advance towards Falaise was resumed". Location: Falaise, Calvados (north of the town) with a precision of 10 km. Location approximate: Point 168 is a map height a few miles north of Falaise; the point is the town of Falaise and stands for the area, with a wider precision. Location support: Stacey names Point 168, a height east of the Falaise road, and does not give a village; Point 159 is described as the southern butt of the ridge above Versainville (p. 249). Commander: Brig. J. M. Blackader, the 8th Brigade commander, who took the division temporarily after Keller was wounded on 8 August (Stacey, pp. 224 and 230).

current_activity: Model takes over Army Group B (and OB West) from Kluge
notes: Event date: Wikipedia's Army Group B page lists Model as commander from 17 August 1944 (Hausser acting 15 to 17 August) and its OB West page lists Model as acting commander from 17 August. The CMH Green Book (Breakout and Pursuit ch. 27 p. 532, 535, row of G018) puts the assumption of command at midnight after 18 August. The sources do not agree and neither is judged better, so both rows are disputed. Event support: the event itself is stated in the cited text (see Event date); only the headquarters place is a representative point. Location support fallback: the point is La Roche-Guyon, the headquarters of claims C0011 and C0202, used as a representative point. Review (German Batch 2 follow-up, 27 October 2026; notes and references only, no value changed): the Lexikon der Wehrmacht (Heeresgruppe B, "Generalfeldmarschall Walter Model 17. August 1944 - Kapitulation") and the Bundesarchiv listing RH 19-IX on the EHRI portal ("17.8.1944: Generalfeldmarschall Walter Model") also date Model's command of Army Group B from 17 August; they are one source family with the Tessin-based Wikipedia list, so the 17 August side of group G018 has one family and the CMH (midnight after 18 August, p. 535) the other. Schramm p. 465 and CMH p. 531 date his arrival at the headquarters to 17 August, a different event from taking over command (see C0933). The group stays disputed with no winner; confidence stays 0.3 because the place is a representative fallback point. Nothing in the dataset says that Model's command ended on 14 September: that date of the old task text is the move to Oosterbeek (see C0934); Army Group B was dissolved on 17 April 1945 (see C0937).

notes: Event date: Schramm, OKW war diary vol. IV, half-volume 1, p. 465 (OCR text): "Am 17. 8. traf" ... "Model im HQu der Heeresgruppe B in La Roche ein" (the OCR garbles "Gen.-Feldmarschall" between the two parts); CMH Breakout and Pursuit ch. 27 p. 530-531: "Model arrived on the 17th with instructions from Hitler to relieve Kluge and become OB WEST and Army Group B commander as soon as he was familiar with the situation"; German Wikipedia, Walter Model: "Am 17. current_activity: Night march from the Seine: in the centre of Amiens by 06:00; the two Somme bridges are taken by 11:00
notes: Event date: 31 August 1944 (Ellis, vol. I, pp. 469, 470). Event definition: On General Horrocks's order the division drives through the night of 30-31 August to Amiens; at 04:00 leading tanks of the 29th Armoured Brigade are three miles south of the town, at 05:00 at its outskirts and by 06:00 in the centre; General Eberbach is captured soon after 08:00 and the two main Somme bridges are taken shortly before 11:00; at 18:00 a brigade of the 50th Division takes over the town (pp. 469-470). Event support: one source family (Ellis, the British official history). Ellis, Victory in the West, vol. I, pp. 469-470: "At four in the morning of the 31st leading tanks of the 29th Armoured Brigade, with infantry close behind them, were three miles south of Amiens"; "Shortly before eleven the two main bridges at Amiens were cap- tured and positions were secured on the far bank". Location: Amiens, Somme (new place) with a precision of 5 km. Location support: Ellis names Amiens and gives the hours (pp. 469-470). Commander: Lt.-Gen. B. G. Horrocks, who succeeded Lt.-Gen. G. C. Bucknall in command of XXX Corps on 4 August 1944 (Ellis, vol. I, p. 400; named again on pp. 453 and 469).

Event support: one source family (Ellis, the British official history). Ellis, Victory in the West, vol. I, pp. 469-470: "The Guards Armoured Division was also across the Somme, seven or eight miles further east"; "By dark the Guards held a substantial bridgehead". Location: Amiens, Somme (new place), standing for the Somme crossing east of the town with a precision of 10 km. Location approximate: the point is Amiens; the bridgehead lies seven or eight miles to the east, along the river. Location support: Ellis places the division seven or eight miles east of Amiens (p. 469).

Location: Picquigny, Somme (new place) with a precision of 5 km. Location approximate: the point is Picquigny, the objective; the division was on the road from the Seine. current_activity: SHAEF assumes direct control of the army group as Montgomery's coordination ends
notes: Event date: Breakout-32 p683: on 1 September SHAEF became operational on the Continent and Eisenhower took personal command of the ground forces, replacing Montgomery as pro tem commander. Event definition: 12th Army Group moves from 21st Army Group's coordination to direct SHAEF operational control; the higher-headquarters chain existed before (SHAEF authority exercised through Montgomery's coordination), so this is a change of channel, not the start of a relationship. Location: last-known position, not shown on the date. The CMH command-post list (World War II by Day) has the army group at Laval from 23 August and at Palaiseau from 3 September (C0489); a 12th Army Group history says Laval in August and Versailles in early September, and Eisenhower met Bradley, Hodges and Patton at Chartres on 2 September (a conference place, not the headquarters). So on 1 September the headquarters was at Laval or on the move to the Paris area; Laval is the last listed place, nine days earlier, with no stronger evidence for 1 September. Relationship: SHAEF operational control from 1 September; the 21st Army Group coordination (C0223) ended 31 August. Event support: high (Green Book, 1 September). Location support: low (last listed command post, nine days earlier).

current_activity: Rundstedt is again appointed OB West; the OB West headquarters moves to Koblenz
notes: Event date: Schramm, OKW war diary (KTB 1944, western theater, p. 364): "1. 9. der frühere OB West, Gen.-Feldm. v. Rundstedt" is named as the man put back as OB West, with Westphal as chief of staff; the same day's entry says "Der OB verlegte sein Hauptquartier nach Koblenz". Event definition: the appointment of Rundstedt (arrival at the Führer headquarters, 1 September); the takeover of command in the main OB West headquarters near Koblenz is 5 September, in the next row, so the two rows are different events and not alternatives. Event support: Rundstedt's reappointment is dated by the war diary; the move of the headquarters is stated in the entry of the same day (1 September) without a time. Location: Koblenz, the place the war diary names for the OB West headquarters, with a precision of 10 km. Location support: the war diary names the town and not a building. Commander: Generalfeldmarschall Gerd von Rundstedt. Context: Model had held OB West and Army Group B together since 17 August; the entry says he was overloaded and the Führer separated the two posts again. Review (German Batch 2 follow-up, 27 October 2026; note only, no value changed): the end of Model's OB West term is described in the note of C0823 (5 September).

current_activity: Returns to Dieppe unopposed after the Germans leave; Operation Fusilade cancelled
notes: Event date: 1 September 1944 (Stacey, p. 300). Event definition: The division returns to Dieppe, where it fought the raid of 19 August 1942: the 8th Reconnaissance Regiment reaches the outskirts early on 1 September and finds that the German rear parties left the day before, so that the Bomber Command attack of Operation Fusilade is cancelled with twenty minutes to spare; the main bodies reach the town during the day. Event support: one source family (Stacey, the Canadian official history). Stacey, The Victory Campaign, p. 300: "On 1 September the 2nd Canadian Infantry Division returned to Dieppe"; "In the course of the day the main bodies of the 2nd Division reached the town". Location: Dieppe, Seine-Maritime with a precision of 5 km. Location support: Stacey names Dieppe (p. 300). Commander: Maj.-Gen. C. Foulkes (Stacey, Appendix G, p. 665: 11 Jan. 44 to 9 Nov. 44).

current_activity: Montgomery is promoted Field-Marshal; General Eisenhower assumes direct command of the Allied armies in Northern France
notes: Event date: 1 September 1944 (Ellis, vol. I, pp. 476, 477). Event definition: On 1 September General Montgomery is promoted Field-Marshal and General Eisenhower assumes direct command of the Allied armies in Northern France; from that day General Montgomery no longer coordinates the American army group, which the dataset records in CR0116 (ending 31 August) (p. 476). Event support: one source family (Ellis, the British official history). Ellis, Victory in the West, vol. I, pp. 476-477: "General Montgomery was promoted Field- Marshal and General Eisenhower assumed direct command of the Allied armies in Northern France". Location: Blay, Calvados (existing place PL0041), where the tactical headquarters stood in late June with a precision of 5 km. Location approximate: the point is the last documented tactical headquarters place; it is not stated for 1 September and the headquarters had moved on by then. Location support: Ellis does not place the headquarters; the nearest earlier row of the unit is Blay, which is a long way behind the front by September. Commander: General Montgomery (Ellis, vol. I, p. 386).

current_activity: Rundstedt assumes command in the main OB West headquarters near Koblenz
notes: Event date: CMH Lorraine Campaign ch. 1 p. 42: "On the afternoon of 5 September Rundstedt assumed command in the main OB WEST headquarters near Koblenz"; CMH Siegfried Line Campaign ch. 1 p. 17-18 repeats "After assuming command in the main OB WEST command post near Koblenz". Event definition: the takeover of command at the headquarters on 5 September; Schramm's 1 September row (reappointment) is a different event. Event support: two CMH volumes by different authors state the day; both are one source family. Location: the point is Koblenz with a precision of 25 km, because the source says "near Koblenz" and gives no village. Location approximate: a town point for "near Koblenz". Location support: both CMH passages name the headquarters only as near Koblenz. Commander: Generalfeldmarschall Gerd von Rundstedt. Review (German Batch 2 follow-up, 27 October 2026; note and references only, no value changed): the end of Model's OB West term. CMH Breakout and Pursuit ch. 32 p. 700: "While Model remained the Army Group B commander, Rundstedt assumed his old post, Commander-in-Chief, West" (5 September). English Wikipedia, Walter Model: "Model retained command of OB West for eighteen days", counted from 17 August, which ends on 4 September; German Wikipedia (Walter Model, succession box): "16. August – 3. September 1944" for Model as OB West, one to two days earlier than the CMH. So Model held OB West from his arrival on 17 August (or the takeover on 18/19 August, group G018) until 4 or 5 September; Rundstedt's reappointment on 1 September (C0822) preceded his takeover on the afternoon of 5 September (this row); the German Wikipedia 3 September is a noted disagreement and is not recorded as a row. Model stayed the Army Group B commander throughout (CMH p. 700).

Location approximate: the point is the town of Le Havre, the objective; the attack came from the north-east and the division headquarters is not named. current_activity: Market Garden: breaks out of the Neerpelt bridgehead for Arnhem; the foremost troops reach Valkenswaard by 19:30
notes: Event date: 17 September 1944, 19:30 (Ellis, vol. II, pp. 30, 31, 34). Event definition: On Sunday 17 September XXX Corps starts north from its bridgehead over the Meuse-Escaut canal near Neerpelt along the road through Eindhoven, St. Oedenrode, Veghel, Grave and Nijmegen to Arnhem, with the Guards Armoured Division leading; after a hard fight with anti-tank guns and bazookas the foremost troops reach Valkenswaard at 19:30 and halt there for the night (pp. 30-31 and 34). Event support: one source family (Ellis, the British official history). Ellis, Victory in the West, vol. II, pp. 30-31: "The road to be taken by Second Army's XXX Corps started from their small bridgehead over the Meuse"; p. 34: "it was 7.30 p.m. when Valkenswaard was reached by the foremost troops". Location: Valkenswaard, Noord-Brabant (new place) with a precision of 3 km. Location support: Ellis names Valkenswaard as reached by the foremost troops that evening (p. 34); the corps headquarters is not named. Commander: Lt.-Gen. B. G. Horrocks, who succeeded Lt.-Gen. G. C. Bucknall in command of XXX Corps on 4 August 1944 (Ellis, vol. I, p. 400; named again on pp. 453 and 469).

current_activity: Market Garden: corps headquarters lands by glider and sets up near Groesbeek; no contact with the 1st Division
notes: Event date: 17 September 1944 (Ellis, vol. II, pp. 34, 35). Event definition: On 17 September General Browning's I Airborne Corps Headquarters, in gliders, is flown in by the Royal Air Force and set up near Groesbeek; communication is established with England and with Second Army but not with the 1st or 101st Airborne Divisions; the corps commands the British 1st and the United States 82nd and 101st Airborne Divisions (pp. 27, 30 and 34-35). Event support: one source family (Ellis, the British official history). Ellis, Victory in the West, vol. II, p. 34: "Browning's I Airborne Corps Headquarters, in gliders"; p. 35: "was flown in by the Royal Air Force and set up near Groesbeek". Location: Groesbeek, Gelderland (existing place PL0686) with a precision of 3 km. Location support: Ellis places the headquarters near Groesbeek (p. 35). Commander: Lt.-Gen. F. A. M. Browning, commanding I Airborne Corps (Ellis, vol. II, p. 30).

current_activity: Market Garden: first flight lands six miles west of Arnhem, on the north bank of the Lower Rhine; about 5,700 men
notes: Event date: 17 September 1944 (Ellis, vol. II, pp. 35, 46). Event definition: On 17 September the first flight of the division lands outside Arnhem on the north bank of the Lower Rhine, its object being the road and rail bridges in the town, but the landing zones are six miles to the west in broken, wooded country; the troops landed include divisional headquarters, the 1st Parachute Brigade and most of the 1st Airlanding Brigade, some 5,700 men; the 2nd Parachute Battalion captures the north end of the road bridge at last light (pp. 35 and 38). Event support: one source family (Ellis, the British official history). Ellis, Victory in the West, vol. II, p. 35: "the first flight of the British 1st Airborne Division had been landed outside Arnhem, on the north bank of the Lower Rhine"; "the areas selected for landing (marked S, X and Z) were six miles away to the west"; p. 46: "The 1st Battalion crossed the railway at Wolfhezen station". Location: Wolfheze, Gelderland (new place), beside the landing zones with a precision of 5 km. Location approximate: the point is Wolfheze, beside the landing zones S, X and Z; the page gives the distance and direction from Arnhem only. Location support: Ellis places the landing zones six miles west of Arnhem (p. 35) and the 1st Battalion crossing the railway at Wolfhezen station (p. 46).

current_activity: receiving the capitulation of German forces in eastern Brest and Recouvrance

Event definition: surrender of the German forces holding Brest and Recouvrance. Ramcke, the fortress commander, had escaped to the Crozon peninsula and surrendered there on 19 September (see the alternate row), so the garrison did not surrender in a single act. Relationship: Ninth Army (VIII Corps passed to it on 10 September).

current_activity: Operation Veritable opens: artillery preparation at 05:00 and the infantry advance into Germany at 10:29
notes: Event date: 8 February 1945 (Stacey, p. 467). Event definition: First Canadian Army opens Operation Veritable early on 8 February: the artillery preparation begins at 05:00 and, after the barrage lifts at 10:29, infantry and tanks pass through the positions of the 2nd Canadian Division to advance into Germany (p. 468). Event support: one source family (Stacey, the Canadian official history). Stacey, The Victory Campaign, p. 467: "The offensive opened early on 8 February"; "At five in the morning the artillery preparation began"; p. 468: "infantry and tanks began passing through the 2nd Division's positions to advance into Germany". Location: Uden, Noord-Brabant with a precision of 5 km. Location approximate: the headquarters place is the one documented on 7 February, not stated for 8 February. Location support: the Army Tactical Headquarters had moved to Uden the day before (pp. 458-459); Stacey does not name the headquarters place on 8 February itself. Commander: Gen. H. D. G. Crerar (Stacey, Appendix G, p. 663: 20 Mar. 44 to 30 Jul. 45). Context: The 1st and 30th British and 2nd Canadian Corps were the corps commanders addressed in the directive that Crerar issued on 25 January (Stacey p. 456); the 3rd Canadian Division fought on the northern flank of the 30th Corps on the first day (p. 471).

current_activity: Veritable: 5th Brigade captures Den Heuvel and Wyler on the Nijmegen-Cleve road; the division is then pinched out
notes: Event date: 8 February 1945 (Stacey, pp. 470-472). Event definition: On the first day of Operation Veritable, added to the formations under General Horrocks for the initial stage, the division, with the task given to two battalions of the 5th Brigade, is to capture Den Heuvel and Wyler and open the Nijmegen-Cleve road to just short of Kranenburg; having completed its limited task it is pinched out of the battle, leaving four divisions to continue the advance. Event support: one source family (Stacey, the Canadian official history). Stacey, The Victory Campaign, p. 456: "at this stage the 2nd Canadian Division was added to the formations under General Horrocks for the initial stage of the assault"; p. 470: "the 2nd Canadian Division had the tasks of capturing Den Heuvel and Wyler"; p. 472: "The 2nd Canadian Division, having completed its limited task, had been pinched out of the battle". Location: Wyler, North Rhine-Westphalia with a precision of 3 km. Location approximate: the point is Wyler, the more easterly of the two objectives; Den Heuvel lies a short distance to the west. Location support: Stacey names Den Heuvel and Wyler as the objectives of the division (p. 470). Commander: Maj.-Gen. A. B. Matthews (Stacey, Appendix G, p. 665: from 10 Nov. 44). Context: The division fought under the 30th Corps for this stage (p. 456); the dates of that attachment are not given, so no command relation to the 30th Corps is recorded.

current_activity: CMH table lists the division under XIX Corps and the Ninth Army again, with the British 21st Army Group attached
notes: Event date: 2 April 1945 (CMH ETO-OB assignment table of the 95th Infantry Division, row of 2 Apr 45: Corps "XIX", Army Assigned "Ninth", Army Group Assigned "12th", Army Group Attached "Br 21st"; the CMH Combat Chronicle R581 has the same entry, "2 April 1945: XIX Corps, Ninth Army (attached to British 21st Army Group), 12th Army Group", and says the division was assembling east of the Rhine at Beckum on 3 April). Event definition: a CMH table lists the division under XIX Corps and the Ninth Army from this date after its row of 31 March under the XXII Corps and the Fifteenth Army; it says nothing about when command was first exercised or where the division fought, and the Green Book (ch. 16 p. 364) has a regiment of the division clearing Hamm in the following days. Relationship: XIX Corps unspecified_subordination (from 2 Apr 45 to 3 Apr 45, CMH table); Ninth Army assigned (from 2 Apr 45, CMH table); 21st Army Group attached (from 2 Apr 45 to 3 Apr 45, CMH table); 12th Army Group assigned (from 28 Aug 44, CMH table). The table entries start on the first row of the unbroken run (convention V-013). The CMH table has a single corps column and does not say assigned or attached for a corps. The earlier operational_control relation to XXII Corps (CR0477) is closed at 1 April 1945 (inferred_from_next_claim); see the Review note on it. Location: Beckum (CMH ETO-OB command-post list, R531 p. 356: listed 2 April 1945); the town centre stands for the command post. Coordinates: Wikipedia (en): Beckum, Germany. Event support: moderate (the CMH table and the CMH Combat Chronicle agree; they are one family). Location support: moderate (command post listed on the date). Review (26 October 2026, found while adding this row): the CMH table row of 4 Apr 45 lists "XIV" in the Corps column and the Combat Chronicle lists XIX Corps until 8 April and XVI Corps from 9 April; no relation to XIV Corps is recorded, and the table-based relation to XIX Corps is made from 2 April to 3 April only (the day before the row that no longer lists it). The Green Book (ch. 16 p. 366) says that the XIX Corps commander grouped the 95th Division, the 8th Armored Division and the 15th Cavalry Group on 7 April into Task Force Twaddle under the 95th Division commander and that General Simpson transferred its operational control to the XVI Corps; the table lists XVI Corps from 9 April. The three sources are not reconciled here. Review (27 October 2026, decided by Scott; changed text): the clause "XIV Corps has no unit record in this dataset" is removed; reason: a unit record US-COR-014C (placeholder, theater pacific) was added on 27 October 2026 at Scott's approval, and the sources read (Wikipedia, XIV Corps) place that corps only in the Pacific, so the table's "XIV" is still not confirmed for Europe and still produces no relation. Review (27 October 2026, decided by Scott; no value changed): Scott approved keeping the relations as recorded, that is the Combat Chronicle version (XIX Corps to 8 April, XVI Corps from 9 April), with this disagreement annotated; old value and new value are the same, and the CMH table's XIV entry for 4 April stays unrecorded as a relation.

current_activity: Corps orders to clear western Holland to the Grebbe Line; the 49th Division's Arnhem assault succeeds quickly
notes: Event date: 14 April 1945 (Stacey, pp. 572 and 574). Event definition: General Foulkes issues new orders to his divisional commanders, confirmed in writing on 15 April, for the corps to clear the enemy from western Holland between the Ijssel and the Grebbe Line; the 49th Division assault at Arnhem has succeeded quickly, so the 1st Division is ordered to link up with it and open the Arnhem-Zutphen road. Event support: one source family (Stacey, the Canadian official history). Stacey, The Victory Campaign, p. 572: "On 14 April, accordingly, General Foulkes in his turn issued new verbal orders to his divisional commanders, confirming them in writing on the 15th"; "1 Cdn Corps will clear enemy from Western Holland between the Ijssel and the Grebbe Line"; p. 574: "quick success attending the 49th Division's assault at Arnhem". Location: Arnhem, Gelderland (existing place PL0553) with a precision of 10 km. Location approximate: the point is Arnhem, the town taken that week; the corps headquarters place is not stated. Location support: Stacey names the 49th Division assault at Arnhem and the corps task west of the Ijssel (pp. 572-574). Commander: Lt.-Gen. C. Foulkes (Stacey, Appendix G, p. 664: 1st Canadian Corps, 10 Nov. 44 to 17 Jul. 45). Context: Only the time in the Western Front theatre is recorded; the corps positions in Italy before this are deliberately not written (Canadian Batch 2 scope).

current_activity: 9th Brigade, the vanguard, dashes through Meppel and Steenwijk towards Leeuwarden on 14 April
notes: Event date: 14 April 1945 (Stacey, p. 556). Event definition: The 9th Brigade becomes the vanguard in a dash from Deventer for Leeuwarden, nearly 70 miles away, riding in borrowed gun tractors and vehicles, and pushes through Meppel and Steenwijk on 14 April; the 7th Brigade occupies Zwolle. Event support: one source family (Stacey, the Canadian official history). Stacey, The Victory Campaign, p. 556: "The 9th Infantry Brigade became the vanguard in a dash for Leeuwarden, nearly 70 miles in a direct line north of Deventer and only ten miles from the coast"; "On 14 April the 9th Brigade pushed on through Meppel and Steenwijk". Location: Steenwijk, Overijssel with a precision of 5 km. Location approximate: the point is Steenwijk, where the leading brigade of the division stood that day; the main body of the division is not placed. Location support: Stacey names Meppel and Steenwijk as the places passed on 14 April (p. 556). Commander: Maj.-Gen. R. H. Keefler (Stacey, Appendix G, p. 666: 23 Mar. 45 to 19 Nov. 45).

current_activity: Operation Cleanser: Hoffmeister issues his orders for the thrust to the Ijsselmeer from his headquarters at Didam
notes: Event date: 14 April 1945 (Stacey, p. 576). Event definition: General Foulkes gives instructions to General Hoffmeister for the quick thrust north to the Ijsselmeer, and Hoffmeister issues his orders on 14 April from his temporary headquarters at Didam, planning to advance from Arnhem through Otterloo and Barneveld to Nijkerk; Stacey gives the afternoon for the instructions and noon for the orders on the same page. Event support: one source family (Stacey, the Canadian official history). Stacey, The Victory Campaign, p. 576: "the 5th Armoured Division was preparing the quick thrust north to the Ijsselmeer, for which General Foulkes gave instructions to General Hoffmeister on the afternoon of 14 April"; "As General Hoffmeister looked north-west from his temporary headquarters at Didam"; "At noon on the 14th Hoffmeister issued his orders". Location: Didam, Gelderland with a precision of 3 km. Location support: Stacey names Didam as the temporary headquarters of the division (p. 576). Commander: Maj.-Gen. B. M. Hoffmeister (Stacey, Appendix G, p. 667: 5th Canadian Armoured Division, 20 Mar. 44 to 6 Jun. 45). Context: Only the time in the Western Front theatre is recorded; the division positions in Italy before this are deliberately not written (Canadian Batch 2 scope).
